questions.questionText: The fluid mosaic model describes the cell membrane as having:

options.text: A fluid phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins

questions.hint: Mosaic of lipids and proteins that can move.
questions.explanation: The fluid mosaic model shows a flexible phospholipid bilayer with proteins that can move laterally within it.

questions.questionText: Which type of molecule is found in the phospholipid bilayer of the cell membrane?
questions.hint: Lipid molecules with a phosphate head.
questions.explanation: Phospholipids have a hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic fatty acid tails, forming the bilayer.

questions.questionText: What is the role of cholesterol in the cell membrane?

options.text: Structural support and regulation of membrane fluidity

questions.explanation: Cholesterol stabilises the membrane at low temperatures (prevents rigidness) and at high temperatures (prevents excessive fluidity).

questions.questionText: Which type of membrane protein spans the entire bilayer?
questions.hint: Goes all the way through the membrane.
questions.explanation: Integral (transmembrane) proteins extend through the bilayer, while peripheral proteins are attached to one side.

questions.questionText: Glycoproteins and glycolipids are important because they:

options.text: Act as cell markers for cell-cell recognition

questions.diagram: Sugar chains on the outer surface.
questions.explanation: Carbohydrate chains on glycoproteins and glycolipids serve as unique identification markers for cell recognition and communication.

questions.questionText: The hydrophobic tails of phospholipids face:

options.text: Inward toward each other in the centre of the bilayer

questions.explanation: Hydrophobic fatty acid tails face inward, shielded from water, while hydrophilic heads face outward toward the aqueous environments.

questions.questionText: The cell membrane is selectively permeable, meaning:

options.text: It allows all substances to pass freely
It only allows specific substances to pass
It allows nothing to pass through
It only allows lipids to pass

questions.hint: Controls what enters and exits the cell.
questions.explanation: Selective permeability ensures specific molecules can cross the membrane while others cannot, essential for homeostasis.

questions.questionText: Carrier proteins differ from channel proteins in that carrier proteins:

options.text: Allow only ions to pass through
Change shape to move molecules across the membrane
Do not interact with the molecules they transport

questions.hint: Think about a revolving door vs a tunnel.
questions.explanation: Carrier proteins bind to specific molecules and undergo conformational changes to transport them across the membrane.

questions.questionText: Peripheral membrane proteins are attached to the membrane by:

options.text: Hydrophobic interactions with the bilayer core
Interactions with integral proteins or phospholipid heads
They are embedded within the bilayer

questions.hint: Located on the surface, not embedded.
questions.explanation: Peripheral proteins attach to the membrane surface through electrostatic interactions or hydrogen bonds, often with integral proteins.

questions.questionText: The 'fluid' nature of the membrane refers to:

options.text: The lateral movement of phospholipids and proteins
The presence of water in the membrane
The passage of substances through the membrane

questions.hint: Proteins and lipids can move within the bilayer.
questions.explanation: Membrane fluidity allows phospholipids and proteins to move laterally within their layer, enabling membrane dynamics and function.

questions.questionText: Which membrane protein type is involved in cell signalling?
questions.hint: Bind to hormones and other signalling molecules.
questions.explanation: Receptor proteins bind specific signalling molecules (e.g., hormones) on the cell surface, triggering intracellular responses.

questions.questionText: Unsaturated fatty acids in membrane phospholipids:

options.text: Have no effect on membrane properties

questions.explanation: Unsaturated fatty acids with cis double bonds create kinks that prevent tight packing, increasing membrane fluidity.

questions.questionText: The glycocalyx (cell coat) functions primarily in:
questions.explanation: The glycocalyx is the fuzzy coat of carbohydrate chains extending from glycoproteins and glycolipids, involved in protection and recognition.

questions.questionText: At low temperatures, cholesterol in the membrane:

options.text: Prevents the membrane from becoming too rigid
Causes the membrane to break apart

questions.explanation: Cholesterol acts as a temperature buffer, preventing the membrane from becoming too rigid at low temperatures by disrupting close packing of fatty acid tails.

questions.questionText: When membrane proteins move and bump into each other and change function, this is called:
questions.explanation: Collision coupling occurs when two membrane proteins physically interact upon collision, potentially triggering a functional response without a diffusible messenger.

questions.questionText: Phagocytosis and pinocytosis are both forms of:
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis (solid particles) and pinocytosis (fluids) are both forms of endocytosis that involve membrane invagination to form vesicles.

questions.questionText: In receptor-mediated endocytosis, what ensures specific uptake of molecules?

options.text: Specific receptor proteins that bind target molecules
The size of the molecule only

questions.explanation: Receptor-mediated endocytosis uses specific membrane receptors that bind only target molecules, ensuring selective uptake of substances like cholesterol.

questions.questionText: The mosaic aspect of the fluid mosaic model refers to:

options.text: The variety of different proteins embedded in the lipid bilayer
The colour of the membrane under a microscope

questions.diagram: Like a mosaic with different coloured tiles.
questions.explanation: The mosaic nature comes from the diverse types of proteins (receptors, channels, carriers, enzymes, structural) interspersed among the phospholipids.

questions.questionText: Lipid rafts are:

options.text: Dynamic microdomains rich in cholesterol and saturated lipids

questions.explanation: Lipid rafts are cholesterol-rich microdomains with unique lipid composition that concentrate signalling molecules and are involved in cell signalling.

questions.questionText: Exocytosis differs from endocytosis in that exocytosis:

options.text: Releases material from the cell; endocytosis brings material in
Is a form of passive transport

questions.diagram: Vesicles fuse with the membrane to release contents.
questions.explanation: Exocytosis moves materials out of the cell via vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane, while endocytosis brings materials in via vesicle formation.
